title: Lesson 7: Giving & Generosity
description: Generosity flows from grace. Through the widow's two small coins and the Jesus who became poor for you, this lesson shows why everything you have belongs to God and how to grow as a glad giver.

blocks.text: In the last lesson, you saw that worship is gladly reflecting back to God the radiance of His worth. Few things show what you think God is worth as clearly as what you do with your money. This lesson is about giving, and it starts with a widow and two small coins.

blocks.title: Two Small Coins
blocks.text:
Jesus sat down in the temple across from the offering box and watched people put in their gifts. Many rich people came by and put in large amounts. It was impressive, and people noticed.

Then a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, worth about a penny. No one else would have noticed. Jesus did. He stopped and called His disciples over.

"Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on" (Mark 12:43-44).

The point is not the amount. It is the heart, and equally, the trust. The wealthy gave from their extra, and she gave from her poverty. She had decided that God was more reliable than the two coins she was holding. That is not foolishness. That is faith you can see with your eyes. And it is worship, declaring with everything she had that God was worth more than her next meal.
Generosity Starts with Grace
Look at where Jesus went next. Within days of watching the widow give everything she had, He gave everything He had. Paul points to that gift when he teaches the church about giving:
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.

Paul does not begin with a rule or a percentage. He begins with Jesus. The Son of God left the riches of heaven and went all the way to the cross, so that you could be rich in Him: forgiven, adopted, and loved forever. You cannot out-give Him, and you do not give to pay Him back. You give because you have been given so much. Generosity is grace flowing through you to others.
Exposing Your Heart

Jesus talked about money and possessions often. He understood something most of us resist: money is one of the most spiritually exposing things we handle. It reveals what we really trust, what we really love, and what we think will keep us safe. Jesus was not against wealth, and some of His devoted followers had plenty. But He was relentless about the heart posture money tends to produce.
No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.

Notice what Jesus did not say. He did not say you should not serve both, or that it is hard to serve both. He said you cannot. Money wants to be your master. It wants your trust when the bills pile up. It wants you to believe your security comes from a number in your account instead of a God who owns everything. Generosity is what happens when God wins that choice, when you say with your wallet what you say with your mouth: He is enough.
7.1 - What do you think it means "to serve" or to "be devoted to" money?
Everything Belongs to God
The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein.

God owns the earth. He owns your house, your car, your retirement account, and your paycheck. You are a manager, not an owner. Think about how many things we "own" that, in a few short years, other people will say they "own": homes, land, possessions, treasures. Stewardship is managing what God owns for God's purposes during the time He has entrusted it to you.
So the question is no longer, How much of my money should I give to God? The question is, How much of God's money should I keep? That is stewardship thinking, and it is freeing.
7.2 - If you are a manager of God's money and not the owner, how does that change the way you think about money?
Why You Give
Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

The word cheerful translates the Greek word hilaros, which means glad or cheerful. Our English word hilarious comes from it. God is not after a guilty giver, a pressured giver, or a giver who gives the bare minimum. He loves a glad giver, someone who gives so freely that it looks a little surprising from the outside, because that is what trust looks like.

Think about three ways people give:

a) The one who gives like paying taxes. She gives because she has to.

b) The one who gives like paying an electric bill. She gives because she ought to.

c) The one who gives like buying a present for someone she loves, like the widow. She gives because she wants to, and she cannot help it.
7.3 - When you give, does it feel more like paying taxes, paying a bill, or buying a present for someone you love?
The Generosity Ladder
Most Christians begin their giving journey giving little or nothing. That is not a reason for shame. It is a place to start. Joy-filled generosity usually grows one rung at a time.

blocks.title: The Generosity Ladder
content: Rung 1: Begin Generosity. Start somewhere. Give first, taking an amount off the top of every paycheck before spending anything else. Many begin at 1 or 2 percent and grow from there. This first step starts reshaping your heart toward money.

Rung 2: Faithful Generosity. Move to planned, intentional giving. Christians have long started with the tithe, 10 percent. Direct your gifts with purpose to your local church, to missions, to the poor, and to needs God places in front of you.

Rung 3: Eternal Generosity. Adopt what John Piper calls a "wartime lifestyle." Consider capping your lifestyle so that when extra resources arrive, you gladly fuel urgent Kingdom work, reaching the unreached and advancing the gospel. Here you discover that God gives more peace and security than money ever could.

blocks.text: Wherever you are on the ladder, the next step up is not about earning God's favor. You already have it in Jesus. It is about loosening money's grip and enjoying God more.
7.4 - Which rung will you step onto this month, and what first amount or percentage will you give?
This Week's Practice

Before your next paycheck arrives, decide on the amount you wrote above and set it aside first, before any other spending. If your church offers automatic giving, set it up this week. Then, as you give, pray a simple prayer of thanks: Jesus, You became poor so that I could become rich in You.
Also this week, read Mark 12:41-44 and 2 Corinthians 8:1-9 slowly. Notice that the widow and the Macedonian churches both gave out of poverty, and that Paul points straight to Jesus as the reason.
Lesson 7 Review

The widow gave everything she had, and within days Jesus gave everything He had. Though He was rich, He became poor for your sake. Because Jesus gave Himself for you, you can give gladly from what is already His. Everything belongs to God, so you are a manager, not an owner, and money does not get to be your master. God loves a glad giver. So take your next step on the Generosity Ladder, and watch money lose its grip on your heart.
In the next lesson, you will see how God's covenant love, the love that gives first, holds your closest relationships together.
Closing Reflections
What is one key thing you learned from this lesson?
What is one step you are going to take this week?
What is a prayer request for this week?
This lesson draws on John Piper's teaching on a wartime lifestyle.
